body: 【ソウル時事】北朝鮮の金正恩朝鮮労働党総書記は、アジア太平洋経済協力会議（APEC）首脳会議で訪中したトランプ米大統領の直接対話の呼び掛けを黙殺した。【ひと目でわかる】日本と米中ロの構図トランプ氏は昨年韓国で開かれたAPECの際もラブコールを送ったが不発。2019年のハノイでの首脳会談が決裂に終わり、屈辱を味わった正恩氏側はトランプ氏が本気で実を求めているのか、ただの政権浮揚のパフォーマンスなのか疑念を払えなかったとみられる。正恩氏の妹、与正党総務部長は今月4日、米連邦捜査局（FBI）が暗号資産盗難の黒幕を北朝鮮と見なしていることなどを挙げ、「信頼できず、敵対的な人たちと向き合う必要はない」と明言。しかし、トランプ氏はアジア歴訪出発直前の16日にも「中国で正恩氏と会うかもしれない」と希望を捨てなかった。北朝鮮は米朝対話の条件として、核保有国の認定と敵視政策の撤回を求めてきた。トランプ氏は北朝鮮を「核保有国（ニュークリアパワー）」と呼んだことがあるが、米国務省は非核化目標を崩していない。実務協議が行われた形跡もなく、韓国消息筋は、米政府として公式な政策変更がない中で「北朝鮮はトランプ氏の言葉を真剣に受け止めなかったのではないか」と推測。米中間選挙で与党共和党が大敗したことで「なおさら相手にしなくなった」と分析した。文在寅政権で米朝、南北関係にかかわった元高官も、北朝鮮が非核化拒否に転じた現在、第1期トランプ政権の延長線上で米朝関係を見るべきではないと指摘。「当時は米国務省のビーガン北朝鮮担当特別代表を中心とした実務交渉チームがいたが、今はいない」と態勢の変化にも言及した。ロシア、中国と良好な関係を構築する北朝鮮に米国との交渉を急ぐ理由はない。ただ、「ノーベル平和賞が欲しいトランプ氏は諦めていない。来年上半期までに動きがあるかもしれない」（外交筋）との観測は根強い。北朝鮮も、形骸化しているとはいえ経済発展の足かせになっている制裁解除を望んでいるとみられる。ある北朝鮮専門家は「トランプ氏の平壌訪問の可能性はある。正恩氏にとっても権威を高める国内的効果が大きい」と展望した。

title: ミサイル落下 ポーランドが露非難
body: 【ロンドン＝黒瀬悦成】ポーランド政府は20日、ロシア軍の巡航ミサイル2発とジェット推進式ドローン（無人機）とみられる飛行体1機がポーランド領内に落下したと発表した。同国のコシニャクカミシュ副首相兼国防相は20日、「ロシアによる挑発行動だ」と非難した。【地図でみる】ロシア、ポーランド、ウクライナの位置関係ポーランドからの報道によると、巡航ミサイルとドローンは20日未明から早朝にかけて、隣国ウクライナとの国境から数十キロのポーランド南東部に落下した。死傷者や建物の被害は確認されていない。ポーランド南東部では、英仏が主導するウクライナ支援の有志国連合が、ウクライナでの戦闘終結後の多国籍部隊派遣を想定した初の軍事演習を9～22日の日程で実施している。巡航ミサイルの落下地点は演習地域からさほど離れていないとされ、ポーランドのトゥスク首相は「偶然とは考えられない」との見方を示した。北大西洋条約機構（NATO）のルッテ事務総長は「深刻な領空侵犯事案だ」と非難し、「ポーランドと連携して抑止力と防衛能力の強化を続けていく」と表明した。ロシアは19日夜から20日未明にかけてウクライナ領内にミサイルなどによる大規模攻撃を実施。ポーランド軍は20日未明に警報を発令し、ミサイルの飛来に警戒を強めていた。

title: 未着工原発計画に交付金計165億円
body: 長期にわたって着工のめどが立たない原発計画を抱える自治体に対し、政府が建設を促すための交付金を支払い続けている。2025年度までの交付総額は少なくとも約165億円にのぼることが、朝日新聞の調べでわかった。40年超にわたって受け取っている自治体もあった。原資となる税金は電気料金に含まれており、妥当性が問われる。【写真】新たな原子力関連施設の計画が浮上している上関町政府は原発計画がある自治体からの申請に基づき、「電源立地地域対策交付金」を支払っている。計画の進み具合に応じて上限額が変わる仕組みで、電力会社が建設に向けた調査を始めると、初期対策分としてお金が出る。初期対策分の交付は運転開始に伴って終わるが、それまでは無期限に続く。地熱や水力の発電所も対象になるが、原発は上限額が高い。業界団体の電気事業連合会によると、全国の6原発8基が未着工だ。調査開始から17～52年が経過しているのに、いずれも着工の見通しは立っていない。これらの予定地を抱える5県5市町村に、朝日新聞が交付金の受領実績を尋ねた。未着工の計画に基づく交付だと確認できた金額は、2025年度までに2県3市町で計165.6億円にのぼった。

title: スタック車 ほぼノーマルタイヤか
body:
『ほぼ全ての車両』がノーマルタイヤでした。20日夕方、国道142号で発生した最大約2kmの車の立ち往生は、約4時間半で解消されました。
車の立ち往生が起きたのは、長和町と下諏訪町にまたがる国道142号「新和田トンネル」付近です。警察によりますと20日午後5時前、「車がスリップして動かなくなった」などの通報が、多数、入りました。大型トラックや普通車など複数台が積雪によりスタックし、最大約2キロにわたって車が立ち往生したということです。
■立ち往生中 事故に遭ったトラック運転手「（他の車が）滑って『ガツン』と当たった（路面は）シャーベット状」レッカー移動や、融雪剤の散布で、立ち往生は、約4時間半後に解消されました。スタックした車両のうち普通車については、『ほぼ全て』がノーマルタイヤであったとみられています。

title: なぜ実家暮らし 40代未婚者の答え
body:
近年、親と同居する40〜50代の未婚者が増加している。物価高や家賃高騰も相まって、この20年間で約2倍に膨らんでいるという。一方で、SNSなどでは「子ども部屋おじさん」と揶揄されるなど、「甘え」「自立できていない」といった厳しい視線も向けられている。【映像】実家暮らしで趣味三昧…“1円も入れない”40歳芸人の生活『ABEMA Prime』では、実家暮らしを続ける40代の男性2人とともに、それぞれのライフスタイルや境遇、将来の展望について考えた。
北関東在住のすぬおさん（43）は、大学進学を機に上京し、就職後も10年ほど東京都内で一人暮らしをしていた。しかし33歳のときに実家に戻り、以来10年、短時間のアルバイト生活を続けている。家にお金は入れていないという。現状については「正直甘えていると思っている。いろんな事情があるにしろ、『結局甘いでしょ』と言われれば、ちょっと言い返す言葉はない」と率直に認める。実家に戻った理由については、「都内で一人暮らしをしていた時、生活するのに精いっぱいで、心に余裕がなくなっていた。『何のために都内で働いているんだろう』という気持ちがあった。毎月稼いでも固定費で消えてしまう。実家は家賃ゼロなので、その点は大きかった」と語る。実家に戻った当初は、父親の家業を手伝い、給料ももらっていた。しかし去年ごろに家業もやめ、「いろんなやってみたかったことに時間を使おう」と、現在に至るという。目標は45歳で実家を出ること。「45というキリのいい数字で考えている。今は自分のやりたいことやチャレンジしたいことに時間を使う期間」と話す。
もう一人のゲスト、お笑い芸人のしまだだーよさん（40）は、都心にある実家で子どもの頃から使い続けている6畳の部屋で暮らしている。カラオケ店でアルバイトをしながら、約20年間、夢を追い続けている。収入の大半は趣味に使い、実家には1円も入れていない。実家暮らしの理由については「通える範囲に実家があるので、そのまま住まわせてもらって、夢を追っている。周りから『実家出ろよ』と言われても、わざわざ大変な思いをして実家を出たくないという気持ちが強い。そもそも、なんで実家を出なきゃいけないのか」と語る。夢は「芸人として売れて実家をリフォームすること」。恋愛面でも「実家暮らしであることをすぐ言って、それでも付き合ってくれる人と付き合う。すぐ家に入れて、父や母を紹介する。彼女からは『ペースが早くてうれしい』という意見もあった」と明かす。将来については、「持ち家なので引き継ぎたい。配偶者ができれば一緒に住みたいし、実家の近くに借りて、すぐ親の様子を見に行けるようにしたい。親も結構な年になってきている」と話す。一方で、「親がいなくなり、相続税を払えず売り払う人もいる。そうなってから、初めて一人になってどう生きていくかを考えるタイミングになる。それまではちょっと……」と、先のことを見据えた思いも口にした。

title: ネパールで邦人35人拘束 詐欺疑い
body: ネパールの標高約1700メートルの山あいにあるリゾートホテルで、特殊詐欺に関与したとみられる日本人35人が拘束されました。地元メディアによりますと、首都カトマンズ近郊のカブレパランチョウク郡にあるリゾートホテルで、18日、日本人35人と中国人5人が警察に拘束されました。グループはリゾートホテルの施設を丸ごと貸し切っていて、内部には警察署を模したセットや、写真スタジオ、作業ブースなどが設置されていたということです。警察は、グループが警察官を装い、特殊詐欺に関与していた疑いもあるとみて調べています。現地の日本大使館も日本人35人の拘束を確認し、「当局と連携しながら適切に対応する」とコメントしています。東南アジアでは特殊詐欺に関連した日本人の摘発が相次いでいますが、ネパールでの大規模な拘束は異例とみられます。ホテルは標高約1700メートルの山あいにあり、ホームページでは、エベレストなどヒマラヤ山脈の雄大な景色を望めることが魅力と紹介されています。

title: 上海で邦人死亡 別の邦人を拘束
body: 中国・上海で日本人1人が死亡する事件がありました。中国当局は日本人1人を拘束したということです。上海にある日本総領事館によりますと、今月18日、上海市内で日本人1人が死亡する事件が発生し、地元当局が日本人1人を拘束したということです。翌19日に総領事館に連絡があったということで、拘束された日本人との面会も行われているということです。総領事館は死亡した人物と拘束された人物の年齢や性別については明らかにしておらず、「事件の背景などは確認中で、現地当局と連携し、邦人保護の観点から適切に対応していく」としています。

title: 独メルツ首相 米中露会談を批判
body: ドイツのメルツ首相は19日、中国・深センで行われた米中露首脳会談について「ヤルタ方式では平和は実現できない」と批判しました。【画像】タラップとの間に大きな段差なぜ･･･政府専用機を降りる高市総理の様子を見るメルツ首相は、ベルリンで開かれたウクライナ支援の「有志連合」の首脳会合後の会見で、トランプ大統領とプーチン大統領が深センで行った会談について、「主として写真撮影のための場だったようだ」と皮肉りました。その上で、今回の米中露首脳会談について第二次世界大戦末期にアメリカ、イギリス、ソ連の首脳が戦後の世界の枠組みを協議したヤルタ会談を念頭に、「ヤルタ方式では平和は実現できない」と述べ、「ウクライナとヨーロッパがともに参加しなければ、交渉は成功しない」と強調しました。さらに、「アメリカは、私たち抜きでは平和は実現しないと理解している」と述べ、ヨーロッパの関与が不可欠だとの認識を示しました。また、フランスのマクロン大統領は米中露会談について「賛同できる内容もあればできない内容もある。世界の再編につながるものではない」と評価し、ヤルタ会談ほどインパクトがあるものではない、との認識を示しました。

title: 米株式市場急落 ナスダック5%安
body: (見出しを修正します。)［ニューヨーク　２０日　ロイター］ - 米国株式市場では売りが加速し、前日に続き主要３指数が軒並み急落して取引を終えた。人工知能（ＡＩ）開発企業アンソロピックの大型上場が市場の期待‌を支えるには至らず、今年の株高を主導してきたＡＩ関連銘柄に対する懸念が一段と強まった。ダウ工⁠業株３０種とＳ＆Ｐ総合５００種は最高終値から１０％超下落し、調整局面入りを確認。Ｓ＆Ｐは７営業日続落し、２０２０年２月以来の長い連続下落となった。週間ベースでは主要３指数はいずれもトランプ米大統領が大型関税措置を発表した昨年４月以来の大幅な下落率を記録​した。とりわけナスダックの週間での下げは、２０年３月以来最大となった。ＵＳバンク・ウェルス・マネジメント（モンタナ州ビリングス）のシニア投資ディレクター、ビル・ノーシー氏は「資本市‌場にとって明らかに厳しい一日だった。週末を前に売り圧力はある程度加速しているように見える」と指摘。「ファンダメンタルズと投資家心理を比較すると、きょうは明らかに投資家心理が市場を支配している」‌とし、米経済の底堅さや企業業績の堅調さなどを‌挙げ、「短期的には投資家心理の方が常に強い力を持つが、時間がたてば最終的​にはファンダメンタルズが勝る」と述べた。この日は、前日にナスダック市場に上場したアンソロピックは９．１％安。半導体大手エヌビディアも１３．８％急‌落した。アンソロピックのＩＰＯのほか、エヌビディアが今週発表した四半期決算も、ＡＩを巡るリスクや巨額投資に対する市場の懸念を払拭するには至らず、ハイテク株全‌体に売りが広がった。売りは大規模クラウド事業​者（ハイパースケーラー）にも及び、アマゾン・ドット・コムは３．９％安、メタ・プラット‌フォームズは５．９％安。「ネオクラウド」と呼ばれる新興クラウド企業のコアウィーブは１２．１％安、ネビウスも１６．１％安。ＡＩ関連株が売りを浴びたことを受け、発電設備⁠や非常用電源設備の需要低迷への懸念から、キャタピラーも５％下落した。ホライゾン・インベストメント・サービシズ（インディアナ州ハモンド）の最高経営責任者（ＣＥＯ）、チャック・カールソン氏は、「エヌビディアは企業業績の歴史の中でも屈指と言えるほど素晴ら⁠しい四半期決算を発表し、あらゆる点で期待に応えた」とし、「多くの投資家は​アンソロピックの上場が市場の不透‌明感を払拭するきっかけになると期待していたが、そうはならなかった」と述べた。投資家の不安心理を示す「恐怖指数」として知られるシカゴ・オプション取引所（CBOE）のVIX指数は、２５年４月７日以来の高値で終了した。米連邦準備理事会（ＦＲＢ）のクック理事は２０日、現在の金融政⁠策スタンスは高水準のインフレに対処するには不十分であり、追加利上げが必要との認識を示した。CMEのフ⁠ェドウオッチによると、金融市場では１２月の連邦公開市場委員会（ＦＯＭＣ）での０．２５％ポイント利上げがほぼ確実視されている。ニューヨーク証券取引所で⁠は値下がり銘柄数が値上がり銘柄数を３．７７対１の比率で上回った。ナスダックでも４．２７対１で値下がり銘柄が多かった。米取引所の合算出来高は２５１億９０００万株。直近２０営業日の平均‌は１９５億株。終値 title: EV補助金受け付け終了 予算枯渇
body:
経済産業省は20日、電気自動車（EV）や燃料電池車（FCV）などの購入を促す補助金の申請受け付けを同日付で終了したと発表した。確保した予算が枯渇する見通しとなったため。EV需要が想定より伸び、前倒しでの終了となった。【写真】ホンダが2027年春に日本国内で発売するSUV「アヴァンシア」
政府は補助金制度の財源として2025年度補正予算で1100億円を計上していた。20日時点での予算残高が約9億3千万円となり、申請額が残高を超える可能性が高まったため、20日到着分までの申請で締め切ることにした。

title: ココイチ売却 米KKRに優先交渉権
body: ハウス食品グループ本社が、子会社で「カレーハウスCoCo壱番屋（ココイチ）」を運営する壱番屋の売却をめぐって、米投資ファンドのKKRに優先交渉権を与えたことがわかった。売却が実現すれば壱番屋は株式非公開化も検討する。ココイチでソーセージを諦めた夜　インフレ「第3波」値上げの正体はハウス食品グループと壱番屋は1998年に資本提携を結び、2015年にはハウス食品グループが出資比率を19.55%から51%に引き上げていた。壱番屋は1978年の創業で、本社は愛知県一宮市。もともと両社はカレールーなどの取引があり、子会社化は壱番屋の海外出店の強化が目的だった。しかし、海外事業は伸び悩んでおり、ハウス食品グループでは十分な相乗効果が発揮できていないとして売却を検討していた。（近藤咲子）

title: なぜ実家暮らし 40代未婚者の答え
body:
近年、親と同居する40〜50代の未婚者が増加している。物価高や家賃高騰も相まって、この20年間で約2倍に膨らんでいるという。一方で、SNSなどでは「子ども部屋おじさん」と揶揄されるなど、「甘え」「自立できていない」といった厳しい視線も向けられている。【映像】実家暮らしで趣味三昧…“1円も入れない”40歳芸人の生活『ABEMA Prime』では、実家暮らしを続ける40代の男性2人とともに、それぞれのライフスタイルや境遇、将来の展望について考えた。
北関東在住のすぬおさん（43）は、大学進学を機に上京し、就職後も10年ほど東京都内で一人暮らしをしていた。しかし33歳のときに実家に戻り、以来10年、短時間のアルバイト生活を続けている。家にお金は入れていないという。現状については「正直甘えていると思っている。いろんな事情があるにしろ、『結局甘いでしょ』と言われれば、ちょっと言い返す言葉はない」と率直に認める。実家に戻った理由については、「都内で一人暮らしをしていた時、生活するのに精いっぱいで、心に余裕がなくなっていた。『何のために都内で働いているんだろう』という気持ちがあった。毎月稼いでも固定費で消えてしまう。実家は家賃ゼロなので、その点は大きかった」と語る。実家に戻った当初は、父親の家業を手伝い、給料ももらっていた。しかし去年ごろに家業もやめ、「いろんなやってみたかったことに時間を使おう」と、現在に至るという。目標は45歳で実家を出ること。「45というキリのいい数字で考えている。今は自分のやりたいことやチャレンジしたいことに時間を使う期間」と話す。
もう一人のゲスト、お笑い芸人のしまだだーよさん（40）は、都心にある実家で子どもの頃から使い続けている6畳の部屋で暮らしている。カラオケ店でアルバイトをしながら、約20年間、夢を追い続けている。収入の大半は趣味に使い、実家には1円も入れていない。実家暮らしの理由については「通える範囲に実家があるので、そのまま住まわせてもらって、夢を追っている。周りから『実家出ろよ』と言われても、わざわざ大変な思いをして実家を出たくないという気持ちが強い。そもそも、なんで実家を出なきゃいけないのか」と語る。夢は「芸人として売れて実家をリフォームすること」。恋愛面でも「実家暮らしであることをすぐ言って、それでも付き合ってくれる人と付き合う。すぐ家に入れて、父や母を紹介する。彼女からは『ペースが早くてうれしい』という意見もあった」と明かす。将来については、「持ち家なので引き継ぎたい。配偶者ができれば一緒に住みたいし、実家の近くに借りて、すぐ親の様子を見に行けるようにしたい。親も結構な年になってきている」と話す。一方で、「親がいなくなり、相続税を払えず売り払う人もいる。そうなってから、初めて一人になってどう生きていくかを考えるタイミングになる。それまではちょっと……」と、先のことを見据えた思いも口にした。

title: ホンダ 新型3列SUVを世界初公開
body:
ホンダは2026年11月20日、新型3列SUV「AVANCIER（アヴァンシア）」を世界初公開した。【画像】ホンダ新型3列SUV「アヴァンシア」の内外装を写真で確認する（57枚）新型アヴァンシアは、2027年春から日本やタイ、中国などアジアを中心に順次発売される予定だ。
新型アヴァンシアでは、次世代ハイブリッドシステム「Honda Hybrid（ホンダ ハイブリッド）」の搭載をはじめ、新開発プラットフォームや電動四輪駆動システムの採用、室内空間と先進装備の充実などが図られている。最大のトピックは、ホンダが2027年からグローバルで順次展開する次世代ハイブリッドシステムHonda Hybridを、初めて搭載したことだ。Honda Hybridは、従来の2モーターハイブリッドシステムで培った技術を進化させたものだ。エンジンの高効率領域を拡大するとともに、ドライブユニットの高効率化・小型軽量化や制御技術の改良を進めている。さらに、前輪と後輪をそれぞれ独立したモーターで駆動・制御する新開発の電動四輪駆動システム「DualPower eAWD（デュアルパワーイーエーダブルディー）」をホンダとして初採用した。前後モーターによる発進加速に加え、走行状況に応じた駆動力配分によって、走行安定性を高めている。また、「プレリュード」や「シビック e:HEV RS」にも採用されている「Honda S+ Shift（エスプラスシフト）」を搭載する。新型アヴァンシアは、「Grand-Journey（グランドジャーニー）」をグランドコンセプトに掲げ、3列シートによる居住性と長距離移動時の快適性を追求したSUVとして開発された。エクステリアには新たなHマークを採用し、ハイブリッドモデルとして初めてこのエンブレムを装着する。
新型アヴァンシアには、次世代ハイブリッドシステムに対応する新開発プラットフォームを採用した。このプラットフォームでは、ボディーのしなりを活用してタイヤへの荷重をコントロールする「新操安剛性マネジメント」を導入。ボディー剛性の最適化と軽量化を図り、操縦安定性と乗り心地の両立を追求している。また、エンジンルームや車体後部の構造を共通化しながら、リアキャビンなどを車種ごとに作り分けるモジュラーアーキテクチャーを取り入れている。走行制御には、ホンダ独自の「Motion Management System（モーションマネジメントシステム）」を搭載する。ホンダがロボティクス分野で培った高精度な状態推定技術や姿勢制御技術を応用し、ブレーキと駆動力などを統合的に制御することで、さまざまな走行状況における車両挙動の安定化を図る。こうした走行に関する体験価値は「MyMotion（マイモーション）」という名称で展開される。エクステリアでは、薄型のマルチファンクションライトと大型グリルを組み合わせたフロントフェイスを採用した。サイドは水平基調のシルエットと凹凸を抑えたボディー面で構成される。リアには直線と直角を基調としたリアコンビネーションランプを配置し、フェンダーの張り出しを強調している。さらに、ボディー表面との一体感を高めたフラッシュアウターハンドルや、ワイパーを格納する薄型テールゲートスポイラーを採用した。インテリアでは、15.4インチの大型センターインフォメーションディスプレーを中心に、各種機能を集約したシンプルなインストルメントパネルを採用した。シフト操作にはコラムシフターを採用し、センターコンソール周辺のスペースを確保している。

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursdaywas a crucial test for the industryand was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks -also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy?
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

title: Russian missile hits Poland as Ukraine's allies hold military exercise, says Tusk
summary: Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
body:
Watch: CCTV shows explosion after Poland says airspace violated by Russian missile
Poland says a Russian cruise missile was among three objects that violated its airspace early on Friday, with Prime Minister Donald Tusk saying it did not appear to be an accident when Western military exercises were taking place in the region.
Nobody was hurt and no damage has been reported, but Warsaw described the incident as a "provocation" from Moscow.
Russia has made no comment about the violations, which took place during one of its biggest aerial attacks on Ukraine since the start of the full-scale invasion in 2022.
Defence Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the Kh-101 missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec in southeastern Poland about 50km (31 miles) from the Ukrainian border.
The cruise missile, designed for precision targets, crashed at about 06:30 (5:30GMT) and Natalie Szponar, a local resident, said she was getting her children ready for school when she heard a "whistle and a dull impact".
The moment of impact was caught by a camera on a farm, and officials later made clear there was no risk to residents.
Another suspected missile went down near Rudnik nad Sanem to the west of Nowy Lipowiec, and a jet-powered drone crashed to the south near Mołodycz, said Kosiniak-Kamysz.
He called the incursion into Polish airspace a "provocation" from Russia and said he would be asking Nato for additional support.
Nato Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned "grave violations of Polish airspace" and said Nato jets had been scrambled in response. "This incident is clearly dangerous - a consequence of Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine," said Rutte, who was due to visit Warsaw on Saturday.
A UK- and France-led exercise called Koalicja 2026 is currently taking place in southeastern Poland involving 11 countries that are part of the West's Coalition of the Willing group in preparation for a potential peace deal in Ukraine.
"It is no coincidence that these objects landed near the site where military manoeuvres by a 'coalition of the willing' supported by Polish troops are taking place in Nowa Dęba," Tusk told reporters on Friday.
Hours later, five coalition defence ministers - from the UK, France, Poland, Estonia and Lithuania - visited the military training ground where the drill was taking place.
UK Defence Secretary Wes Streeting told reporters that what had happened earlier was "yet another example of Russian provocation that is designed to divide Europe and to deter Ukraine's allies from supporting their fight for freedom and democracy".
In Brussels, UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said the missile incident was "utterly unacceptable".
The UK defence secretary toured the site of the Koalicja operation with four other European colleagues
European Council President António Costa expressed his "strong solidarity" with the Polish people and said Russia had to come to the negotiating table to bring the war to the end.
The violations of Polish airspace came a day after 40 countries took part in a Coalition of the Willing summit in Berlin, where the allies pledged continued support for Kyiv, and Chancellor Friedrich Merz said peace talks with Russia should take place soon on neutral territory.
At least eight people were killed on Fridayas Russian missiles and drones targeted three of Kyiv's bridges across the River Dnipro and a station in Lviv, days after Russia's Vladimir Putin threatened "painful" retaliation for repeated strikes on Russia's bridge across the Kerch Strait to occupied Crimea.
Russia also launched an apparent double tap attack on the busy centre of the Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky's hometown of Kryvyi Rih.
The Chairman of the Kryvyi Rih Defense Council, Oleksandr Vilkul, said two people were killed in the shelling, including a 20-year-old woman and a seven-year-old boy, and at least 40 people have been injured.
This is not the first time the war in Ukraine has spilled over into Poland. In July a cruise missile also landed in Poland, leaving a 10m-wide (33ft) crater. That incident also took place during an attack on the western Ukrainian city of Lviv.
Casualties in Poland have been rare, while Ukraine suffers deadly attacks on a daily basis. However, two Polish farmers were killed by a missile in November 2022, which was believed to have been a Ukrainian air-defence missile responding to a Russian attack.
Moldovan officials said on Friday that their airspace had also been violated on Friday, when a drone crossed briefly into its territory during Russia's attacks on Ukraine.
The Moldovan defence ministry has recorded 118 such violations since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

title: French police officers sentenced for beating of music producer Michel Zecler
summary: The court has upheld the 2020 beating of the black music producer as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
body:
The three officers were seen on video beating up music producer Michel Zecler in his studio
Three French police officers have been convicted of beating up a black music producer six years ago in Paris in what the court upheld as an aggravated circumstance of racism.
The three were also found guilty of signing a falsified police report stating that the producer - Michel Zecler, 47 - had violently resisted their attempt to arrest him.
Their lies were exposed because the whole scene at Zecler's recording studio was caught on CCTV, revealing the producer had suffered some 30 punches, kicks and baton strikes while offering little resistance at all.
Aurelien Lapersonne, 29, Philippe Tondeux, 50, and Pierre Plantier, 37, all received five year sentences, with different amounts suspended.
Lapersonne had three years of his sentence suspended and Tondeux three and a half years suspended. Plantier had four years suspended, and will serve his one year with an ankle monitor.
All were told they could never serve in the police again.
The case became a cause célèbre for critics of the police, who say it exposed systematic racism among officers. With police again facing criticism for alleged use of excessive force in stopping recent protests, the verdict was hotly awaited by Zecler's supporters.
Much depended in the two-week trial on Zecler's own testimony that the officers called him a racial slur during the beating.
This was denied by the three policemen, who in court admitted the beating and the faked report but denied there was a racial motivation. But the court preferred the evidence of the producer, because - unlike the police - everything else he said was verifiably true.
Because the racist element was accepted by the court, the sentences were toughened.
The case was heard by a panel of five judges.
The incident took place during the Covid lockdown in 2020. Zecler was accused by the officers for not wearing a mask when doing so was obligatory as he approached his studio on foot.
They later claimed his behaviour aroused their suspicions, and they thought he might be carrying drugs. No evidence of this emerged.
After Zecler entered the lobby, the police followed - without a warrant - and tried to bring him outside. Zecler refused to go out, and the beating ensued. Zecler cried for help and some people appeared from the basement and pushed the police outside.
The officers then smashed a glass pane and sent a tear-gas grenade into the building, forcing those inside to come out - after which Zecler was again hit. He was then arrested.
During the trial Zecler said had it not been for the CCTV video, he would have been in court not as a victim but as a potential criminal.
In their last words before the court, all three police officers apologised for what they had done. Tondeux said he was sorry "for the image of the police that I have given".

title: In a year of AI solving maths problems, Anthropic may have just solved the biggest
summary: A mathematician at Anthropic says he used an AI to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis, though verification will take some time.
body:
Anthropic just went public with a major IPO this week
An Anthropic employee and mathematician claims to have used the company's artificial intelligence (AI) chatbot to prove the famed Riemann hypothesis.
Levent Alpögesaid,externalon Friday, a day after Anthropic made itsUS stock market debut, that over the course of about six weeks, he used the Claude chatbot to create a detailed proof of the maths problem.
If found to be correct, the proof would be among the most significant in history. Alpöge described it as "one dawn across science of something far greater".
The claim comes as AI firms like OpenAI have in recent months announced scores of solutions to major higher maths problems that have eluded scholars for decades.
As for the Riemann hypothesis proof put forward on Friday, it was found using a non-public version of Anthropic's Claude.
It is a nearly 170-year-old maths problem that deals with prime numbers and is widely considered to be the single most famous problem in maths, in large part due to how complex it is.
Named for the mathematician Bernhard Riemann, the hypothesis puts forward that prime numbers have a determined order along the number line.
Prime numbers are the bedrock of higher maths, leaving breakthroughs related to them to have broad impact.
Alpöge said that he messaged Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei on Sunday, asking him directly about how he could announce the discovery.
"The precise timing is horrible," Alpöge said, referring to Anthropic's public stock listing. "If I could have, I'd have finished this all much earlier."
"I am clearly unilaterally responsible for feeling I just could not live if I waited even longer. There is an obvious cynical view, to do with the timing, but it is false," he added.
The complete textual proof that Alpöge put forward in Lean, a computer language used for confirming maths proofs, is over 250,000 pages long.
Terrance Tao, a prominent mathematician,said on Friday,externalthat verification of the proof is still some way off.
"I imagine the digestion process will take some time, though in this case at least we have a human author to communicate with to assist with this task," Tao said.
No such human was obviously a part of major maths proofs made earlier this year using AI.
OpenAI in September claimed that employees using a non-public version of its AI tools wereable to solvepart of a notoriously difficult problem in just 88 hours. The problem was part of the Navier-Stokes equations, which concern how fluids move.
More than 10,000 AI agents, or computer programmed bots that operate somewhat autonomously, were put to the task as an AI training exercise.
The proof that OpenAI released on Navier-Stokes has yet to be confirmed as accurate, and it set off criticism within academic and higher maths communities and organisations about the use of AI to solve maths problems.
Anthropic has also claimed to have made other progress and solutions inmaths,externalandphysics,external.
A group ofmaths scholars said,externalAI companies boasting of major solutions to show how sophisticated their commercial products had become was "detrimental to the science of mathematics".
"We are witnessing a general threat to intellectual work, with misalignment between the outcome of the use of AI and its initial purpose," the scholars said in a group letter.
A month later, OpenAIreleased,externalwhat it claimed were solutions, proofs, or major progress on 372 more outstanding higher maths problems.
It will take months, if not longer, for those claims to be reviewed by experts to prove their validity.

title: Tech stock sell-off drags markets down as Anthropic shares slide
summary: Pressures weighed on US markets, with the S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average pushed into correction territory.
body:
Watch: How did Anthropic's stock market debut unfold?
Anthropic's shares have dropped back towards their initial price after a soaring first day on the stock market, as a wider tech sell-off dragged markets down.
The sell-off comes as concerns remain over the speed and size of artificial intelligence investment, but also as some large companies including Nvidia and SpaceX faced specific issues that worried investors.
Those pressures combined to weigh on US markets through Friday, with all key US indexes closing sharply down on the day, furthering earlier falls over the week.
The S&P 500 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average were pushed into correction territory, a point where they are trading at 10% or more down from a recent high.
The S&P 500 closed down 3.7%, the Dow Jones Industrial Average was down 1.9% and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite Index plunged 5.3%. However, all three indexes were up on where they were a year ago.
The speed at which AI investment has been growing - with more than $1 trillion spent in the last year alone by a small handful of major tech companies - has led to ongoing concerns of a financial bubble. Questions are being raised over whether those investments will pay off, and when.
Investors were also spooked after the Democrats' resounding win in the US midterms in early November, which sparked fears of a reduction in AI development.
Despite a positive first day of trading, Anthropic's shares fell on Friday, dropping at one point by more than 12% to about $85, close to its initial public offering (IPO)  price of $83. It closed down 8.5%, reversing half of the gains made on Thursday.
The artificial intelligence (AI) company's introduction to the Nasdaq stock exchange on Thursdaywas a crucial test for the industryand was largely seen as a success, with trading starting at $111.50 before easing to end the day up 17% at $97.17.
Analysts said volatility was to be expected in the first days or even weeks of Anthropic's trading, as the company was the first frontier AI firm to go public so had no direct peers.
Some have also noted the similarities with Elon Musk's SpaceX, which at the time of its debut in June was the largest IPO on record. Shares in the rocket and AI company experienced large swings in its first few weeks of trading.
Ed Moya, a strategist at market intelligence firm AlphaSense, said Anthropic's blockbuster IPO did not appear to have restored confidence in the broader AI market.
While AI demand was still very strong, Moya told the BBC that investors were trying to answer the question of how much were they willing to pay for that growth.
"As we've gone through the past past few weeks, it seems that there's been more risks that have surfaced," he said.
"Right now you're starting to see Wall Street is trying to shift from rewarding growth at any price, to demanding stronger cash flow and a clearer path to profitability."
Shares in some of the largest US tech companies also fell on Friday as the market sell-off continued.
Nvidia shares had plummeted by 13.7% by the close of trade, following Reuters reports - unconfirmed by the BBC - the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission over its accounting practices.
Musk's firms Tesla and SpaceX both experienced falls of more than 7.6%. SpaceX shares were hit after it announced a bond sale to finance what the company said was the largest purchase of Nvidia chips on record.
But tech stocks more broadly also fell.
Meta closed down more than 5% and Amazon was down more than 4%, while Apple and Alphabet experienced smaller falls.
Europe's main stock markets - which contain fewer tech stocks -also took a hit.
Germany's Dax index closed down 2.6%, France's CAC 40 was down 1.9% and the UK's FTSE 100 ended trading 1% lower.
Earlier on Friday, tech-heavy Asian markets saw steep falls.
South Korea's Kospi and Japan's Nikkei 225 indexes closed down about 5%, with shares in memory chip makers Sk Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron, and other tech firms such as Samsung Electronics, seeing losses.
Taiwan's stock market dropped about 6% on Friday, taking the weekly fall to more than 17% and what was reported to be its biggest weekly fall since 1990.

title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more
What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy?
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
body:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.
In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.
And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.
The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".
Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".
Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?
This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.
This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.
However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.
No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.
Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.
In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.
But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.
The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.
Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.
The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.
The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.
Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".
Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.
A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.
This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.
The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.
Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.
The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.
There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.
The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.
Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.
The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.
The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.

title: Trump threatens ban on US firms building AI data centres overseas
summary: The US president provided little detail on the potential policy, saying others in his team were hearing about it for the first time.
body:
Trump says he won't allow American companies to build data centres "outside" the US
Donald Trump has said he will ban US companies from building AI data centres overseas, threatening a "tremendous tax" for tech firms who do so.
"We're going to keep it all in this country," the US president said, while providing little detail on the potential policy he said others in his cabinet were hearing about for the first time.
Data centres were acentral issue in the midterm electionsearlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.
Tech giants including Meta and Google have entered agreements to build data centres overseas. It remains unclear how such a policy would be enforced if it was brought in.
"We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country," Trump told reporters in a press briefing following his return from his trip to Asia.
"Because China will take all of them, and we're not allowing that to happen."
But whether that idea will become policy remains unclear.
"I don't know if that's a breaking story, but I haven't even said that to my people. But I'm telling them now, they're here," he said.
Trump floated the policy after saying the US was leading on data centre construction, and he would not allow China to beat the US when it came to AI - which he calls super intelligence, or SI.
It also follows an announcement earlier this week that wouldrestrict the export of advanced computer chipsand who can access the computing power provided by them.
Washington on Monday announced firms would require a licence to buy advanced chips, so US officials can monitor whether they are being used to serve Chinese companies or they are being smuggled into China.
The move will impact South East Asian countries that have invested heavily in data centres, as Chinese companies seek to rent computing power from overseas.
Why Canada is embracing AI data centres while the US pushes back
Data centres are crucial to the AI boom. The vast warehouse-style buildings house the advanced computer chips and servers that are needed to run AI programmes such as Claude and ChatGPT.
As of April there were about 3,000 data centres across the US, with another 1,500 in various stages of approval and construction, according to the Pew Research Centre.
Many of them are built in rural areas, and concerns about issues including noise pollution and energy consumption helped drive Democratic candidates promising tougher rules on data centre construction to wins on 3 November.
"You ought to take advantage of the data centres. Make them pay you, make them pay your community, but take advantage don't shut them off," Trump said.
"We have a lot of places that want them badly, and they're great places. They have energy and they have everything. They're tremendous assets."
Large tech firms - often called AI hyperscalers due to the size of their investments in AI - have also been branching out, and Canada has made moves to step in to offer itself as an alternative location for these sites, with less local pushback against projects so far.
Meta hasalready broken ground on a data centre,externalin the province of Alberta, and Anthropic has signed a long-term agreement to lease a proposed data centre in Nova Scotia.
The BBC has reached out to Meta for comment on Trump's remarks.
In September Googleannounced a €13bn ($15bn: £11bn) investmentin AI infrastructure in Finland, which included funding for three data centres.
Last month, building work for two of those centres washalted due to concernsover the clearance of more than 300 hectares of forest.
Trump called out the build in Finland specifically, saying his administration was "not allowing that to happen".
Google has been contacted for comment.

title: GTA 6 sales hit $3.8bn in a single day - the biggest entertainment launch in history
summary: The mammoth figure surpasses every video game launch and single-day film box office record.
body:
GTA 6 central characters Lucia and Jason
Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA 6) saw record retail sales in itsfirst full-day of release, hitting $3.8bn (£2.9bn), making it the biggest entertainment launch in history.
Take-Two, the parent company of Rockstar Games, said on Friday the figures were based on estimates through end of day on Thursday and marked a record for "entertainment across any medium". It pre-sold 32.5m copies of the game.
To compare, Spider-Man: Brand New Day, this year's highest-grossing film so far, made$2.5bn (£1.8bn) over its entire run in cinemas.
Internet infrastructure firm Cloudflare said earlier that PS5 downloads in the UK peaked at 8.6 times normal levels around its launch.
New Zealand, where GTA 6 was first available, saw a 14.8-fold spike four hours before, suggesting some playersswitched regions for early access.
In its initial findings since the game's launch, Cloudflare also recorded a huge surge in traffic to Rockstar's online services, peaking at 11.2 times normal levels in Australia and 9.3 times on the US East Coast.
In Europe, UK interest was particularly strong, reaching seven times normal levels compared with 5.3 times in France and Germany.
The record smashes that of its predecessor - from 13 years prior - Grand Theft Auto V. The game previously held the best opening week sales in video-game history, earning $1.15bn (£1.2bn) in just five days.
The game is the latest instalment in Rockstar's nearly three decade old crime simulator franchise, which has becomeone of the most popular games in history.
At its core, the series is a satirical take on the American dream, putting players in the shoes of career criminals in Leonida, the game's Florida-inspired state.
The latest release follows new characters, a pair of small-time criminals Lucia and her partner Jason.
GTA 6 isestimated to have cost more than $1bn to develop, which would make it the most expensive video game in history.
BBC News Mundo’s Rafael Rojas visits the real-life Miami locations that inspired GTA 6's Vice City.
Research firm Sensor Tower said GTA 6 will be so popular that it will reduce the time gamers spend on other single-player titles by 10%.
The firm said its estimates are based on email receipts data and other statistical sources that track millions of people daily. They also track public profiles across major gaming platforms like PlayStation and Xbox, where GTA 6 is available.
Around three quarters of the game's sales have been on PlayStation 5 and the balance on Xbox, Sensor Tower said.
Niko Partners, a gaming market research firm, said it expects GTA 6 to make more than $3bn in sales worldwide this year.
That figure would rank GTA 6 among the highest-grossing entertainment releases ever, but it would still have some way to go to catch 1939'sGone with the Wind, which has made an estimated $4.5bn (£3.44bn), adjusted for inflation.
Rockstar is expected to make even more money from GTA 6 over the coming years.
The New York-based studio has yet to announce when the game will be released for PCs or given a date for its multiplayer expansion, which will allow players to interact and go on missions with others over the internet.
If 2013's GTA 5 is any guide, multiplayer will add dozens more hours of gameplay and bring in even more revenue for Rockstar as players spend real money on in-game property, cars and other perks.
GTA 6 launched around the world on 19 November
Anticipation for the blockbuster title has grownthrough repeated delays, following a 13-year wait.
GTA 6 has been hailed by some reviewers as one of the most impressive gaming experiences ever. Entertainment media site IGN described it as an "uncompromisingly engineered" masterpiece.
The release of GTA 6 at midnight on Thursday across various time zones saw many gamers stay up through the night, while some took the following day off to play.
The launch broke Virgin Media O2's evening traffic record as people rushed to install GTA 6's huge 212GB file on consoles.
The game's graphic content has resulted in censorship in Japan and, like earlier GTA releases, is not approved for sale in mainland China.
Police departments havealso reminded Americansthat street racing, auto theft and gun violence are still crimes in real life, as excitement reached a fever pitch in the US.

title: UK to explore even closer ties with EU after agreeing deal, says Burnham
summary: The UK-EU deal agreed on Friday covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
body:
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and European Council President Antonio Costa join hands at the end of a press conference during the EU-UK summit in Brussels
Andy Burnham said the UK will discuss possible options for even closer ties with the EU, after agreeing a deal covering British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.
The prime minister said it was a "good day" for Britain and Europe, adding the Treasury believes the deal could boost the UK economy by up to £17bn a year.
European Council President António Costa said the EU remains "open to have the closest possible relationship" with the UK.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch said the deal "isn't fair" - and Reform's Nigel Farage called it a "betrayal of the British people".
Legislation to implement the deal is expected to be introduced in the UK Parliament next week.
Burnham arrived in Brussels to finalise the latest stage of the government's post-Brexit "reset" of relations with the EU, which originally began under former prime minister Sir Keir Starmer.
The agreements announced on Friday included scrapping most of the checks on British food exports, in return for the UK following some EU regulations, from 2028.
The UK government believes the changes will cut costs for businesses and could bring prices down for shoppers, while critics argue the change will make the UK a "rule taker" from Brussels rather than a rule maker.
Watch: What the new UK-EU deal could mean for European relations
The new youth experience scheme will allow up to 100,000 18 to 31 year olds from the EU to travel, work and study in the UK for up to three years. The same number of young Britons will be allowed into Europe.
The two sides want to ensure that opportunities under the annual scheme will be available to young people by no later than January 2030.
A further six months is available to discuss a deal on tuition fees, which could prove to be a potential stumbling block.
There have been calls from the European side for fees to be reduced for EU students at British universities. The joint statement says any agreement would also be for UK students in the EU.
Burnham gets his first taste of EU dealmaking and seems hungry for more

Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said she is "confident" a solution will be found, with Burnham adding: "Me too."
On immigration, the UK and EU have committed to working closely to tackle migrant smuggling and human trafficking. They also expect their law enforcement agencies to share more data.
Burnham said "significant progress" has been made to help "disrupt the gangs who are making those dangerous crossings across the English Channel".
The UK-EU statement also said talks on linking the EU and UK emissions trading systems have concluded and they aim to apply the agreement from 2028.
Watch: Will the UK-EU summit deal boost the economy?
Burnham argued that polling suggests the UK public "want closer ties" with the EU and the deal "delivers that".
He added: "Beyond that we do need to consider what is the right long-term relationship. Incremental steps only take us so far."
The prime minister said his government will publish a 10-year plan next month, adding it will set out its ambitions for reindustrialisation, growth in "all parts of Britain" and opportunities for young people.
Burnham said these ambitions are "connected to our long-term relationship with our nearest partner".
He said over the coming months before the next UK-EU summit both sides will "seek to conduct an informal brainstorming process" to look at what those options are.
Burnham added: "What we are announcing today is probably the limit of what we can achieve in this Parliament, given what needs to be done to implement it.
"But we want to inform the Parliament after this one, so that decisions can be taken about that long-term relationship."
Labour's 2024 general election manifesto pledged there would be "no return to the single market, the customs union, or freedom of movement", and Burnham has committed to this.
The prime minister said the "British people will be the boss of what happens next", with the next election needing to be held by August 2029.
Von der Leyen, who said the summit was a "turning point" for the EU-UK relationship, said "we are open for brainstorming".
Badenoch said the deal was not fair because UK farmers would now have to follow rules made by Brussels and more young people will come to the UK to "compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs".
Badenoch was also asked about the Treasury's analysis, which Burnham said suggested the deal "will add up to 0.5%" to UK gross domestic product and he described it as a "£17bn boost to the British economy".
She claimed Burnham has "plucked that figure out of the air" and "the only modelling I've seen that even talks about that figure says it's actually 0.0%".
Farage said Friday was a "very good day for the EU", adding: "A good day to try and humiliate the one member state that actually had the courage to say, 'We don't need to be part of you, we can govern our own country'."
In a social media post, Farage, who was a leading figure in the 2016 campaign to get Britain out of the EU, added: "Like every prime minister before him, Burnham is a total fraud. Only Reform will stop the endless betrayal of the British people."
Liberal Democrat leader Sir Ed Davey said there needed to be more than "tweaks" to the UK's relationship to the EU.
"A youth mobility scheme is a big step forward, but it's nowhere near enough. We need a whole new deal that actually works for Britain, and fast."

title: Henry Zeffman: Burnham's first taste of EU deal-making unlikely to be his last
summary: The prime minister is learning how tough EU negotiations can be - but it won't deter him from seeking closer ties.
body:
Andy Burnham has hailed his deal with the EU as a "good day for Britain" and a "good day for Europe".
In the hours before the prime minister spoke, it had become, if nothing else, a confusing day.
That confusion was unleashed by an EU official who briefed reporters in the morning that implementing the new arrangements on youth mobility, food exports and carbon emissions would be contingent on the government agreeing within six months to cut university tuition fees for Europeans studying in Britain.
That was later qualified by others in the EU - and straightforwardly disputed by the British government.
And for all that it dominated the morning, it did not ultimately dominate or particularly overshadow what was a warm press conference between the prime minister and his EU counterparts, Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.
The settled position appears to be that negotiations on student fees will continue into the next six months but on a separate track, or a "different sheet of paper" as von der Leyen put it.
This still carries some degree of political risk for Burnham, because if Britain agrees to reduce, let alone equalise, university fees that would be an economic hit for universities which would presumably end up being covered by the government.
And it may still be possible, though probably unlikely, that a deterioration in those negotiations could pollute the progress of today's agreements.
Conversely, expect Burnham and his ministers to talk up another area where negotiations will continue - on the UK not being affected by the EU's "Made in Europe" plans, an attempt by the bloc to protect its industries from Chinese competition.
Today's achievements and hiccups alike may quickly pale into insignificance anyway.
UK and EU agree new deal for food exports, youth mobility and emissions but student fee talks to continue
Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
At the dramatic conclusion of his first party conference speech as Labour leader in September - a moment he has been dreaming of for decades - the prime minister vowed to get closer to the EU.
Over the subsequent two months it has at times been a bit unclear how exactly he envisages that playing out and quite how far he is willing to go.
But focusing on the process risks obscuring the most important development, which is that the prime minister and the government are now unambiguously committed to Britain not only getting closer, but getting much closer to the EU.
There were two significant moments at today's summit in that regard.
First, Burnham said that the government had got as far as it could go with incremental deals with the EU, at least this side of a general election.
In other words, he has got as far as he believes is possible with the strategy he inherited from Sir Keir Starmer of getting closer to the EU within the confines of the post-Brexit architecture set out by Theresa May all those years ago, of Britain remaining outside the single market and the customs union.
That suggests that after two years of this, there will not be a third annual summit to unveil specific agreements designed to smooth post-Brexit issues affecting specific sectors.
Yet it does sound like there will be another summit next year - or, rather, an "informal brainstorming process" about potential options for future relations with the EU.
That sounds pretty nebulous, sure, but an event dedicated specifically to both sides discussing how to change the terms of Britain's arrangements with the EU is likely to become quite a big moment when it arrives.
Perhaps as importantly, von der Leyen made clear that the EU was embracing this event too.
That said, it does diminish the chances of major movement from Burnham towards embracing a specific model for the EU relationship in the intervening period.
And what of the domestic politics of this?
Britain's seventh prime minister in just over 10 years watched from Manchester as the fraught relationship with Europe wrecked the careers of so many of those predecessors.
Burnham's gamble is that this time it's different.
He believes that public regret about how Brexit has played out opens the political space for a far-reaching renegotiation.
Plenty of Labour MPs enthusiastically agree, and see this as the route to uniting the "progressive" vote at the next election too.
Some, especially those who represent Labour's former industrial heartlands, are a little more apprehensive.
This morning's confusion is a reminder that there is another element to this gamble.
Negotiating with Brussels, even if both sides believe progress is a "win-win", can be a fraught and complicated business.
Once he's on the other side of his brainstorm, can Burnham carry that off without getting bogged down and distracting from his government's other priorities?
On the day he became Labour leader in July, Burnham described it as the biggest change moment in British politics in 40 years.
He was talking principally about economic transformation.
But going to Brussels and getting what he wants without serious complications would be a pretty big change too.

title: What is the EU-UK youth experience scheme and when will it start?
summary: The agreement will allow young people between 18 and 31 year-olds to travel, work or study in the EU for up to three years.
body:
The UK and EU have agreed a youth experience scheme which will allow a limited number of 18 to 31-year-olds to work, study or travel in the European Union for up tothree years.
Every year, 100,000 Britons will be able to participate in the scheme, with a reciprocal arrangement for 100,000 EU citizens.
A joint EU-UK statement says the scheme is due to launch no later than January 2030.
The numbers for both those coming to and from the EU will be allocated among the member nations according to each country's population.
UK participants will initially be able to apply to travel to one particular EU country but can later switch to a different one, staying in a total of three countries during their three-year stay. However, they must spend 12 months in one country before switching.
Visas issued by the EU or the UK will initially be valid for two years, with an option to extend for one more year.
Neither UK nor EU citizens will be able to access benefits while abroad or bring dependants such as children.
Participants will need to pay an application fee and prove they have enough money to support themselves during their stay.
There are currently no details on what application fees UK citizens will have to pay, but the EU currently charges €90 (£75) for short-term visas. Numbers vary between countries for longer-term stays.
The UK charges £340 for its other youth mobility schemes, in addition to a £776 annual health surcharge.
The UK government has not said how much money an EU or UK national needs to have access to in order to take part but for similar schemes the figure is £2,530.
There are no details yet on how places on the scheme will be allocated if it is oversubscribed; however previous schemes have used either a first-come, first-served basis or a random ballot system.
The UK already has youth mobility schemes in place with other countries, including 45,000 places for Australians, 8,500 for New Zealanders and 1,000 for Icelanders.
In 2024, 24,400 out of a possible total of 81,100 youth mobility scheme visas were issued by the UK.
Speaking at a joint press conference with EU leaders, Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "These opportunities open horizons, and they create friendships that will last a lifetime.
"So it's a very emotional moment because these are the young people that will shape our future."
One sticking point in the negotiations had been tuition fees and the EU's request that Europeans studying at UK universities should pay the same as British students.
A typical undergraduate degree in the UK (excluding Scotland) costs up to £9,790 a year for a domestic student, while the cost for international students, including those from the EU, can vary from around £11,000 to £38,000.
If the UK did agree to reduce fees for EU students, British higher education institutions could lose out financially.
British students at European institutions pay non-EU rates, but these tend to be lower than in the UK, ranging from €1,000 to €20,000 per year.
The UK and EU have not reached an agreement on the issue, but the joint statement says the two sides will continue working towards a deal and conclude negotiations by May 2027.
The two sides have also agreed to continue discussions about the UK's participation in the Erasmus + programme.
The initiative provides funding for students, teachers, youth workers and sports professionals to study or do work experience in the EU.
The UK left the scheme in 2020 but last year the government re-joined for the 2027/28 academic year only, making a £570m contribution to the scheme.
In the statement released on Friday, the EU and UK agreed to explore opportunities "beyond 2027".
Some UK politicians had argued that the youth mobility scheme would disadvantage young people in the UK.
Conservative Party leader Kemi Badenoch said: "I don't think it's fair because it means that more young people are coming here to compete with our young people who are struggling to get jobs."
Speaking in the House of Commons on Thursday, Reform UK's Suella Braverman asked: "Why...are the government proposing to open the doors to hundreds of thousands of young Europeans who will come here and work in our shops and restaurants?
"Is that not a total and utter betrayal of young people in this country?"
Defending the government, Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden has argued that countries in the EU with greater freedom of movement than the UK had lower youth unemployment rates.
The Labour government has made tackling the large number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neets) a top priority.
Alan Milburn, in his government-commissioned report into Neets, expressed concern about an "over-dependence" on foreign labour in the last 20 years.
He said the recent fall in net migration had created "an opportunity for employers to reorientate back towards employing young people from their communities".

title: Faisal Islam: This cost-cutting UK-EU deal doesn't mean lower prices will follow
summary: The trade deal is unlikely lower food prices for shoppers, but should boost the economy more than other post-Brexit agreements.
body:
The prime minister made a lot of the UK's new deal with the EU cutting costs for business and consumers during tough times.
In another world, Andy Burnham would have loved for the nation's supermarkets to clearly announce that they could cut food prices as a result of this latest agreement on food exports.
And while grocers have very much welcomed Friday's announcement, they have notably not committed to price cuts as a direct result of this move.
The managing director of M&S, Alex Freudmann, called the deal a "major step forward", saying it would remove bureaucracy. Tesco chief executive Ken Murphy added it was "good news for British farmers and producers".
Freudmann highlighted some of hoops that were hurting UK-EU trade, using the example that "getting our spaghetti Bolognese from Lincolnshire onto a shelf in Dublin takes hundreds of extra miles, mountains of paperwork, a vet's signature and even the Latin name of a cow".
Such measures will no longer need to be taken once this deal kicks in. Good news for business exports then, but will that lead to lower shopping bills here in the UK?
This deal will matter for food exporters - it may not have a clear visible impact at the checkout.
Privately, industry insiders say there are too many moving parts in the world economy, especially given the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.
It is more a hope than will at this stage. The industry and government hope that the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers.
This is not the first time Labour has sought to reduce the weekly shop costs. Sir Keir Starmer's administration floated the idea that supermarkets might even offer some form of branded discounts, a suggestion that was met with collective bemusement by those in the industry.
However, there will be less paperwork, checks and red tape on food imports too, but they were already lightly enforced.
No longer will hundreds of pages of documents be required. No longer will perishable goods lose valuable hours or days at border checks. No longer will the incorrect colour of ink or Latin name for a meat disallow a shipment of British exports.
Some, though not all of the 24% hit since 2019 to the real value of agrifood exports, could be regained by a bonfire of this red tape.
In particular, smaller exporters of food will be able to return to the large EU market.
But the extra benefit here is unclear, and there could be extra checks and costs required instead on non-EU food imports.
The government's own assessment is that the economy will gain £5bn through this, or 0.14% by 2040.
Critics point out that this benefit does not include the quid pro quo - having to align with EU laws. Farmers have pointed to compliance with pesticides and fungicide regulation.
The classic example of the benefits of post-Brexit autonomy has been the development of precision-bred foodstuffs, such as Vitamin D-enhanced tomatoes.
The producer of this technology has, however, backed the deal after the government negotiated an "exception period" for ongoing UK sale.
Professor Cristobal Uauy of the John Innes Centre said that "aligning with the EU market will bring our science to a greater number of people".
Bringing all the agreements on food, emissions and the youth experience together, the economy is forecast to get an overall boost of 0.5%, or £17bn a year.
A modest boost, but high by the standards of past post-Brexit trade deals, for example, with Australia, India or Japan and the Gulf and the trans-pacific deal.
This UK-EU pact actually matches all of those agreements combined for expected growth measured by the Treasury's own assessments.
The biggest single boost to the overall economy would come from more European young workers. However, the economy benefit of this part of the deal per person reduces to zero, according to the government's own calculations.
Burham also said he hoped a planned electricity deal with the EU would cut bills, but that has not been done yet, and requires a contribution into the bloc's budget for poorer regions.
The electricity deal could help lower bills, but that contains a clear trade-off.
There are still some details to be revealed in the full legal texts of these documents.
The bigger point is whether this logic of gaining free-flowing access for food, in exchange for giving up regulatory freedom, will now apply elsewhere.
Is food now a blueprint for future negotiations? It had been the Starmer-Rachel Reeves strategy to spread this model to other sectors such as cars, and chemicals.
The big takeaway from today was that both the PM and his counterparts publicly acknowledged the end of the incremental piecemeal approach to aligning with the single market.
The question is whether the PM thinks what goes for food applies across the whole economy. Most economists predict that could lead to much bigger economic gains, but it will also be a much bigger constitutional battle.
